Mr. Speaker, it is always a very satisfying experience for a Liberal to speak about social security. Bearing in mind what the Liberal party has accomplished in this field in the last 25 or 30 years, it is always easy to speak about this matter pleasantly and calmly.
Long before the birth of the Canadian socialist party there were, in the ranks of the Liberal party, men who were thinking about the development of social security in this country. It is with great pleasure that I refer to the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King who, as early as 1900, was giving serious thought to social questions in Canada, and founded our first Department of Labour.
In 1917, long before the appearance of the socialist party in this country, Mr. Mackenzie

Family Allowances Act King wrote a book which has, I am sure, provided a source of inspiration to our socialists. This book, entitled "Humanity and Industry", defined for the future that very social legislation on which we pride ourselves today. In 1927, in order to carry out his ideas on the development of social security, Mr. King had parliament adopt the Old Age Pensions Act. About 1936 followed more social security legislation which was to transform this country's approach to economic problems and increasingly demonstrate to our people that social problems as such were among the first matters to be provided for in the Liberal party's platform. At that time Mr. Mackenzie King brought in the Bank of Canada Act. By thus controlling our credit, Mr. King set his footsteps firmly along the road leading to the economic transformation of this country.
On reading this interesting book by Mr. Hutchison about Mr. King, one becomes aware of the extent to which this great far-seeing statesman has influenced this country's and the United States' policy, since it is said that he influenced Roosevelt's New Deal policy. There is cause for pride if one stops to consider what the Liberal party in this country has done by way of social security and industrial legislation.
In my constituency alone, $3,600,000 was distributed last year for social security, in old age pensions and family allowances alone. Furthermore, I note that in my constituency, thanks to the Unemployment Insurance Act, $600,000 was distributed in the form of unemployment benefits. All in all, the Liberal government has re-established the equilibrium which must exist among all classes of society and it has distributed the money where it was needed; it has acted in such a way that our children, our old people and the sick may enjoy the security to which they are entitled.
We are in favour of social security; it is indeed an object of satisfaction and pride to us Liberals. The present policy, which we have been moulding these last thirty years, is essentially a social security policy. It is because of this that today, in all parts of Canada, people of all ages, religious faiths or beliefs endorse the policy of the Liberal party. Let us develop our resources for the benefit of all Canadians. However, our immense natural resources are and must be developed through private enterprise. It would be bad for our country to kill this spirit of initiative through overtaxation.
I believe that every member of this house and everyone in this country recognizes the good will of the Liberals in trying to settle

this social problem in terms of security for all. A Liberal whose heart is in the right place cannot help but understand that it is necessary to pass legislation to ensure that those who have nothing may live a life that will make them proud of being Canadians.
That is something we all want, we Liberals. We have a long-term program that will, within a very short while, provide our disabled people with a little joy and sunshine. Our social security program is such that the government will be able to bring into effect necessary health insurance legislation. There are many Liberals who believe that we must always go forward, but cautiously. It is quite easy for certain political opponents to confine themselves to outbidding the social security program by asking that it be doubled or tripled, but I believe also, Mr. Speaker, that a certain middle course approach should be our aim in this field as in others.
At the present time, family allowances cost this country $350 million.; to double that amount would mean an outlay of $700 million. Apart from the children who benefit from family allowances, there are those invalids who come to see their member and say: "How is it that the government seems to ignore us? How is it that we seem to be considered as outcasts in our own country? You pass legislation in favour of old people and children, but what about us who are penniless and who are out in the streets?" I think that one of the first legislative measures to be adopted in this country, at the present time, should be in favour of these invalids.
Mr. Speaker, one could speak at some length on this social security question. It is a subject on which a lot has been written in every country. But if we consider what has been accomplished in this country these last 25 years and what has been done in the United States and elsewhere, we find that, thanks to the genius of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, our country is ahead of practically every other country, because of our decision to distribute the wealth of the nation among all classes of our population.
Well I believe that the great advantage of the Liberal policy is this: it is a middle-of-the-road policy. We sympathize with the socialist party people who feel pity for the poor and who want to help them, but they should not think that they are the only ones to have such feelings. We, also, sympathize deeply with all those unfortunate people who ask the government for assistance.
If we were able to double the amount of family allowances, if we could give to our population the benefit of all the social

measures possible we would do it with pleasure. I for one believe that people with means should help the poor.
Mr. Speaker, I notice it is six o'clock. My voice is getting hoarse and I move the adjournment of the debate.
